title: Backspace string compare → without allocating
label: ag-multi
statement: `#` means backspace. Given two strings typed into empty editors, return whether the final texts are **equal**. Backspace on an empty text does nothing.
provenance: Reported as the easy question in an Agoda Senior Software Engineer interview (LeetCode Discuss, ≈ mid 2025) and listed for Agoda on CodeJeet. Stage 2 is the standard follow-up: O(1) extra space.

prompts.label: Check my design — no code
prompts.text: I believe walking both strings from the end with a skip counter finds the next surviving character in each, so the comparison needs no new strings and O(1) extra space. Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: `#` means backspace. Given two strings typed into empty editors, return whether the final texts are **equal**. Backspace on an empty text does nothing.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- Backspace on empty text? (No-op.)
- Null strings? (Treat as empty.)
- Is O(n) extra space acceptable? (Stage 1 yes; stage 2 no.)

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: A # only ever affects characters before it, so reading from the right tells you immediately whether a character survives: count pending backspaces and skip that many.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md: I would say, before coding: "W."alking both strings from the end with a skip counter finds the next surviving character in each, so the comparison needs no new strings and O(1) extra space."

learn.title: 10 · Tests
learn.md:
**S1 — Compare**

- ab#c == ad#c
- ab## == c#d#
- a#c != b
- backspace on empty is a no-op

**S2 — No allocation**

- equal after backspaces
- allocated … bytes (< 65,536 — O(1) extra space)

learn.title: 11 · AI usage strategy
learn.md:
- Make the design decision yourself, then ask the assistant to attack it.
- Delegate the mechanical parts only after the structure is fixed.

**Prompts for this question:**

- *Check my design — no code* — "I believe walking both strings from the end with a skip counter finds the next surviving character in each, so the comparison needs no new strings and O(1) extra space. Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?"
- *Review, do not rewrite* — "Review my implementation for correctness and edge cases. Do not rewrite the code. List problems most severe first, each with the input that triggers it."
- *Race conditions* — "Now review this implementation for race conditions if multiple threads call Compare concurrently. For each race, give the interleaving that breaks it. Then name the smallest synchronization boundary that preserves correctness. Do not write code yet."
- *Tests that expose bugs* — "Suggest tests that could expose bugs in my implementation: boundaries, duplicates, empty and invalid input, and concurrency where it applies. For each, say why the expected value is correct."
- *Complexity check* — "What is the time and space complexity of each public method as written? Do not claim a bound unless every step achieves it."
- *Requirement change* — "The requirement changed: Compare must not allocate in proportion to the input: under 64 KB allocated for two 2-million-character strings. List which members need to change and which do not, before writing any code."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- Building both strings and calling it O(1) space.
- Using a Stack<char> then string.Concat — allocates.
- Forgetting that ## can delete across characters already skipped.
- Index underflow when backspaces outnumber characters.
